title: Havana and Viñales: Showing Your Attitude

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know stance and focus adverbs such as *francamente* and *en rigor* from B2 Unit 1, and also *lamentablemente*, *precisamente* and *apenas*. A stance adverb steps outside the action and comments on the whole sentence. Describing a city is a good place to use them, because you often want to say how you feel about what you see: that something is a pity, or that, strictly speaking, a date is not what people think.

sections.title: Stance and focus adverbs at work
rows: Lamentablemente, algunos edificios están en mal estado.
*lamentablemente*: your feeling about a fact (a pity that...)
En rigor, el pueblo de La Habana existía desde 1514.
*en rigor*: strictly speaking, you give the exact truth
Precisamente en esas tierras rojas se cultiva el tabaco.
*precisamente*: exactly there, pointing at what follows
*apenas*: barely; no commas, it sits right before the verb

items.spanish: Lamentablemente, algunos edificios de La Habana Vieja están en mal estado.
items.english: Unfortunately, some buildings in Old Havana are in poor condition.

items.spanish: En rigor, el pueblo de La Habana existía desde 1514 en otro lugar de la costa.
items.english: Strictly speaking, the town of Havana had existed since 1514 in another place on the coast.

items.spanish: Precisamente en esas tierras rojas se cultiva un tabaco muy apreciado.
items.english: It is exactly in those red lands that a much-appreciated tobacco is grown.

items.spanish: Francamente, la visita a la fortaleza no me convenció.
items.english: Frankly, the visit to the fortress did not convince me.

sections.content: Try the comma test you know. If you can put commas round the adverb, it comments on the whole sentence: *Lamentablemente, ...*. Right after the verb with no commas, the same kind of word usually describes how something was done: *Habló francamente*. *Precisamente* and *apenas* take no commas.
